subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not aware you were looking for a new role in this Chamber but the chair suits you.
I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-27, an act dealing with privileges and immunities of foreign missions and international organizations. The bill repeals two existing statutes, namely the Diplomatic and Councillor Privileges and Immunities Act and the Privileges and Immunities International Organizations Act.
I agree with the Minister of Labour that Bill C-27 permits for the first time certain privileges, immunities and benefits to be granted to political subdivisions of foreign states.
Article 2(1) defines a political subdivision as a province, state, territory, dependency, or any other similar subdivision of a state. It will also provide for extended privileges and immunities to international organizations.
The minister will be happy to learn that my party urges quick passage of this bill for it brings about, at long last, a series of legislative changes that will make Canada a
Government Orders
better place for foreign missions and international organizations.
If Canada's diplomatic missions and those of its provinces have generally been well received abroad, it is in large part due to the extensive privileges and immunities the missions of other countries have been granted in Canada, and we take pride in that. However, Canada's remarkable reputation can only be enhanced by the provisions included in this bill, long sought by various foreign parties such as the International Civil Aviation Organization and the Government of Hong Kong.
Allow me to dwell on a few of them in the next few minutes and suggest ways in which they can be implemented. First, on behalf of my party I applaud the additions of new measures that deal with the duty of the receiving state to ensure maximum protection of the councillor posts. Canada has had its share of tragic incidents in this respect, such as the attack on the Turkish Embassy a few years ago. This time of revolutionary change abroad no doubt can and has been accompanied by massive, sometimes violent manifestations at home.
There is a need to offer all necessary protection to foreign missions established in Canada. As an example, the consular offices of Poland are situated in Etobicoke-Lakeshore next to my riding. During the early 1980s, when martial law was imposed on Poland, there were enormous demonstrations and attacks on the Polish consular offices in Etobicoke-Lakeshore. I must compliment the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Metropolitan Toronto Police Force on their protection of the property of that consular office and their protection of the people working in that consular office. What a pleasure it is now to see people going in and out of that consular office with no demonstrations. The same people who were demonstrating are now using the services of that consular general office.
That being said I want to stress that the legislative authority extended to the Canadian government and its police officers in this bill to protect the premises of foreign missions should be exercised with caution and according to the terms of our charter of rights.
I also welcome the entrenchment of statutory authority of the Secretary of State for External Affairs as a result of increased powers to promote reciprocal treat-

Government Orders
ment and to implement mutually beneficial arrangements.
While our missions have generally been treated well abroad this provision, if used appropriately, may provide the necessary negotiating tool to increase the privileges and immunities now accorded to Canada's diplomatic missions.
Third, I support the provision that provides for additional privileges and immunities to international organizations such as ICAO located in Montreal and the ones we have already mentioned. It is only fitting that then-senior representatives and members of their families be treated like diplomats, a practice that has long been established in most countries over the world.
Perhaps, had this bill been introduced at an early time, an international organization such as the International Maritime Satellite Organization, IMARSAT of Great Britain, an important international organization with 500 employees, might have moved to Canada. The Minister of Labour already mentioned other organizations which could benefit from this bill, organizations such as the Commonwealth of Learning in Vancouver and the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization.
I hope the government will want to use the new measures in a pro-active way by enticing large international organizations to locate their headquarters in Canada.
Fourth, and most important, I welcome the new provision that will permit certain privileges, immunities and benefits to be granted to political subdivisions of foreign states, such as provinces, states, territories and republics, a word I am throwing in purposely.
Part III of the bill introduces legislation that is new to Canada. Presently our government cannot offer reciprocal treatment to offices of a state's political subdivision in Canada because the Secretary of State for External Affairs has no statutory authority to do so.
Political subdivisions in which offices of Canadian provinces could be granted a consular type of status have little incentive to establish consular offices in our country without the possibility of being offered reciprocal status here. I am informed that Hong Kong, a British dependency, has granted special status to provincial offices in its territory. It has been authorized to open a
commercial office in Toronto but refused to do so until Bill C-27 is in force, since a Hong Kong office could only then be accorded reciprocal privileges, immunities and benefits.
The word "benefits" is used throughout this bill. The government could improve or fine tune the bill by defining "benefits". Reciprocal benefits could be anything under the sun. We are creating unnecessary future difficulties by omitting the definition of benefits. Perhaps we could discuss this when we move to Committee of the Whole.
The granting of reciprocal privileges, immunities and benefits to political subdivisions of foreign states is a change which the Liberal Party fully supports and which meets Canadian interests. It is not enough simply to declare that Canada will give better treatment to the foreign missions of substates. These changes will only bring the increased co-operation and open the necessary opportunities if it is used for that purpose by the Canadian government.
To a large extent the relevance of these changes will depend on the Canadian government's recognition that it has failed to seize many opportunities and that it requires an urgent and comprehensive review of its foreign policy. It makes little sense, for instance, to have the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the minister of industry touring the Soviet Union if these contacts are not based on development of a solid framework on which to develop our relationships.
I want to ask the minister: Is he going to implement this provision with respect to Ukraine? As we all know the representatives of Ukraine, with whom our critic, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and I have met on numerous occasions, have developed long grievances over the inaction of this government on its request for the opening of a new office in Ottawa. This is not to mention the abysmal delay in the opening of our own consulate in Ukraine. Now that it is open, let us not delay in opening a reciprocal office in Canada.
Article IV of the Vienna convention on consular relations outlines how a consular post gets officially recognized. Bill C-27 is silent on the procedure of how an office of a political subdivision would become recognized. Can the minister explain why the bill is silent on this since it is a severe offence under the bill to misrepresent any premises as an office of a political
October 4, 1991

subdivision of a foreign state? The process for having such offices recognized must be clarified in the bill.
While I am on the subject of clarification, can the Minister of Labour, on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, clear up the ambiguity of the use of the word "state" in Part III of the bill? In the interpretation section of the bill first use of "state", for an example, that could be a state of New York in the U.S.A., and the second use it would mean a federal type state.
Let me just enlarge upon that and read the exact definition because I feel this is very important when we get to the committee of the whole.
Article II reads, under the interpretation clause:
"political subdivision" means any province, state, territory,
dependency or any other similar subdivision of a state.
The first use of the "state" is a different meaning than the second use of "state." The second use of "state" could be a county of New York. The first "state" could be, yes, New York state, and then the second part could be part of New York state. So I think we need that clarified and fine tuned.
The French does not appear to have that problem because-

"subdivision politique" Province, Elat ou dependance d un Etat ou
toute autre entite similaire de celui-ci.

In the French translation they use the word celui-ci, and in the English they use "state." I think that is where the confusion lies.
My colleague from Quebec compliments me on my French. I am learning. I am getting there.
The world is changing very quickly. New independent nations are springing up around us. Many dependent republics of today will be independent nations tomorrow, yet Canada lacks resources in our embassy in Moscow, has paid foreign mission tokenism in the Baltics, lacks presence in Latin America, and is dragging its feet in eastern Europe.
Our critic, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, was in Moscow recently for the CSCE conference where he met with representatives from around the world. He tells me that other countries are not respond-
Govemment Orders
ing to recent changes in an ad hoc reactive fashion, but are seeing incredible opportunities in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe, and are seizing them. We are not.
While their interest in various parts of the world remains strong, the means by which we pursue those interests are too limited, and too fragmented. For this bill to bear fruit, it must be utilized to reflect the changing realities emerging in Europe and the Soviet Union, to reflect the importance of developing special relationships with new, yet to be bom, nations of the world and to enhance the particular advantages of Canada.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I noted that this is your first occasion in the chair since I have been here, and this is my first occasion to carry a bill, so between the two of us things might go wrong this afternoon.
I must start by admitting that this bill is not exactly a hot topic of conversation in Oshawa. We are a little involved with the Eric Lindros controversy, and we know a lot about the NHL draft, but we are not really as hep about various Geneva conventions as we might be.
I was interested, as I went through the research on the bill, to find some touch points. Sometimes in this world it is strange that things which appear on the surface not to have any impact on you or your life really do affect you.
As I went through the briefing notes on the bill and the research that has been prepared for us on it, it become quite clear why everybody should be in support of this legislation. As one goes through the different parts of the bill one can see some concerns that I would think would be legitimate about the status of people who work in offices such as this and the privileges that are accorded to them. As one gets deeper into it, one is reminded that this is kind of the way that the world has worked out its agreements on this matter. This is not a matter that Canada can change unilaterally on its own. There are ways and means to do that. This bill proposes to put in place some means of regulating what happens when someone else representing an agency comes to Canadian soil and wants to set up and do whatever it is it does.
To that extent, I think all of us in the Chamber should understand that this is becoming increasingly important in our daily lives. Many of us, I am sure, would think that this is part of the diplomatic corps and does not have much to do with the life and times of people in our

October 4, 1991
Government Orders
ridings. However, more and more people are concerned about what happens in different parts of the world. More and more of our industrial sectors are now starting to contemplate what they could do in a country that is trying to rebuild, that is trying to put in place a different kind of an economy.
It occurred to me that several local business people have come to me and talked about doing business in nations in which two years ago it would have been unthinkable for them to do so. But now there are opportunities there. Although there are the regular diplomatic channels which they could pursue, these are people who do not normally move in those circles. Therefore, it would be of assistance to them to have a labour organization there, a commercial organization there, someone that they know from the province of Ontario, for example, to be able to go and work on an exchange program.
There are interesting concepts that are being discussed currently, ways in which investors can go to several European countries where a year ago it was forbidden. They were communist bloc nations and it was not really possible to do much in the way of business transactions there. Now they are very open to such transactions and they need some offices such as the ones that would be covered under this bill to facilitate that exchange. This might involve the province of Ontario establishing an office that could assist in the Ukraine, for example. It might involve someone from one of those states or provinces establishing an office in Canada where they could readily get information.
All members, if they reflect on it for a while, will understand that this is becoming increasingly important as the world becomes more of a mobile place where ordinary citizens can and do move around a great deal and where there is a need for information on what is happening somewhere else in the world or in your own community and that information is needed in a hurry. Anything that facilitates or regulates that or essentially makes it something that is recognized and dealt with by Canadian law-there is an established pro forma way to go about it so that it can happen-is a good thing. That is essentially what this bill does.
I noticed as I went through some of the briefing notes enclosed with the bill that there are some interesting technical aspects of what role is expected of a police
officer in providing security, for example, at one of these offices. It is something, I think, many members would have been involved with at different levels of government. Often the reason one cannot do what is so apparently necessary is that there is no legal provision to do so. If that sounds kind of stupid, that is because sometimes that is the way the law works. If there is not a specific law which outlines how an office is set up and recognized in Canadian law what everybody's legal obligations are, then it is questioned from time to time as to whether one can provide what would be seen as very normal and natural security provisions to an office of this kind.
On the surface the bill looks like something which would not affect anybody who might live in the riding of Oshawa, but as the member I think I could give a pretty good case that it will. On the surface it looks as if this is something that has to do with conventions struck in Vienna some time ago. I am aware that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and several other of our provinces have agonized for many years now over just how they go about setting up an office in Washington, London, or in several other parts of the world; how to get trade and consular offices put in place; and how the various organizational groups that are playing a supportive role get established, identified and recognized under law.
Essentially what this bill does and what I find eminently supportable about the bill is that it provides a piece of framework legislation for Canada, and that makes sense. It acknowledges that such organizations exist, and that makes sense. It limits and restricts somewhat, for some of them, the kinds of provisions that would provide them with immunity. That has to do with whether they pay taxes or not, whether or not they can carry back and forth confidential information. All of these I know to be areas where there has been some confusion before, where there have been occasions where it is the absence of a law which prevents something very sensible from happening.
On those grounds, we find the proposal in Bill C-27 to be eminently supportable. We may have a question or two as we go through the committee stage, and I hope the minister will indulge us if we simply do not understand the language which has been used. He will have the advantage of staff and briefing notes, which we do not have to provide us with clarification.
October 4, 1991

So, with those small provisos, Mr. Speaker, you and I have made it through our first occasion this afternoon.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee, Mr. Hopkins in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Order. House in Committee of the Whole on Bill C-27, an Act respecting the privileges and immunities of foreign missions and international organizations.
Shall Clause 2 carry?
On Clause 2-Definitions

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I need your advice that this is the order to make recommendations, suggestions, et cetera. As I mentioned in my debate, I think we could improve upon the bill.
First, we said something about benefits. I wonder if the minister could explain why benefits are not included. Under the conventions and in the schedules attached to the bill, there is talk about privileges, et cetera, but benefits is a new introduction. It is probably a good introduction, but I think we need some clarification on that.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my colleague from Park-dale-High Park wishes to improve the bill and therefore wants to know what is meant by the word "benefit".
What we mean by benefits is giving access to certain rights which we have as Canadian citizens under our legislation to the people who would come here. For instance, the right of access to property if it were denied by someone or if, for instance, our access to property in a foreign country was made exorbitant or impractical by that one, that would give us the authority. In a sense I cannot call them negative benefits, but they are benefits which they should get and the federal government would be in a position to grant the benefits that you and I have to people coming over here.
It is there as a protective measure for the federal government, not that at this time we have no plans to use that section, for example access to universities or access to schools by these people, is a general clause that would
Government Orders
allow the government to do things in case they are needed.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
I thank the minister for that explanation. Under the Vienna convention they use the wording of facilities, privileges and immunities. I thought those kinds of benefits might be covered here. If they are not, I can appreciate maybe why the wording has been changed. I like creative thinking. I like our country being the first to bring in some changes.
The second item I would like to bring to the minister's attention is again what I mentioned in the debate, the use of the word "state". Article 2(1) reads:
Political subdivision means any province, state, territory,
dependency or any other similar subdivision of a state.
If we look at the United States of America, we can say that political subdivision means any state such as Florida, and then a similar subdivision of that state would be a smaller unit of Florida, whether it is a regional government or a county. It could be very dangerous if we do not amend this.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Parkdale-High Park is quite right, I believe, to raise the issue.
The word that we use in this legislation is the word "state". What we mean is the same meaning that is in the state immunity act. It is the word that is used internationally.
I know it creates a technical problem, but the French version is a lot clearer. Obviously, for instance, if we are talking about the Americans we are referring to New York State and not Clinton County, which would then ask us for a reciprocal arrangement under this legislation.
The member was quite correct. When we talk about states it would be a state but the French word, just because of the word itself not because of the legislation, is clearer. But the hon. member did not raise that in his speech at second reading.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can accept the minister's explanation that political subdivision means any state, to use the example of New York State. However the same phrase goes on: "or any other similar subdivision of a

October 4, 1991
Government Orders
state". Now we are looking at a subdivision of New York State. Could you tell me what that subdivision would be?

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext: We do not mean to refer to a subdivision of New York State. When we refer to states, if we are talking about Americans we refer to states. If we are talking about Germany, we refer to landers. If we are talking about Switzerland, we refer to cantons. It is not our intent whatsoever to include parts of states when we refer to states.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext: I almost feel that this bill should go to a legislative committee just to iron out things like this. I can substitute the word lander in Germany, which is what Germans use, and it would read that the political subdivision means any lander or any other similar subdivision of a lander. Does this mean that we would have reciprocal immunities, privileges and benefits for smaller units of a state such as a subdivision of a lander?

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
I realize that the language of the State Immunity Act might not seem clear. However, I read 2(1) in English and 2(1) in French, and in French it is quite clear. It is quite clear subdivision politique, province, Etat ou dependance d'un Etat ou toute autre entite similaire de celui-ci.
It is not our intention under this legislation to provide for reciprocity with, as an example, part of an American state. When we read both sections it is quite clear. I think the confusion may be a result of the use of the word "state". There is the same problem when using the word "nation" in French, which creates problems for people who talk about the Constitution.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext: We are anxious that this bill be passed as quickly as possible. However, I leave it to the government to look at it again and make it clear through its notes of explanation or whatever. This would not stand up in a court of law, and I leave that to my lawyer friends in the House.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have two questions that were raised by a member of diplomatic personnel here in Ottawa.
First, about the GST. It seems this government requires the tax to be paid, and there is a refund after several months, I don't know how many. I therefore wish
to ask the minister whether this bill will affect that particular issue?
At the same time, perhaps he could answer another question. The same diplomat told me recently that the present government in Canada asks diplomats when they arrive in Canada whether they can specify how long they intend to stay in this country.
Could the minister inform the House whether this bill in any way affects the two issues I have just raised?

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
This bill does not affect the GST whatsoever. Our policy is that it is done in a reciprocal way.
When countries do not charge a similar tax in their country, we do not charge the people who are here. It is done in a reciprocal way. It does not apply to every one of them.
As for his second question, which was do we ask them how long they will be here when they come here, generally when diplomats or consular officials come here we are told the period for which they are coming. It is done in a flexible way and very often the governments will renew their length of stay in the country.
However, we do have a policy which would prevent people from coming here and staying for the rest of their lives, for very long periods of time. Generally people are here for approximately three years. Obviously we have to be flexible on the issue but we still have that policy.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, the diplomat in issue indicated that as far as he knows Canada is the only country that demands to know in advance how long diplomat x or y will be staying in Canada.
He said that it was contrary to both the Vienna convention which deals with that matter and the practices of all other industrial democracies. Maybe the minister has a further comment on that.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext: Madam Chairman, I have just stated the policy. If there is a specific case, such as the case that my hon. friend has mentioned, I would certainly be willing to look into it and discuss it with the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, will the minister tell us if the bill deals with the question of the Russian federation, Ukraine or other members of the former Soviet Union. If for example we receive an application
October 4, 1991

tomorrow from the Russian federation or Ukraine, as we might well, to send an ambassador or a representative to Canada, would this bill affect that in some way?

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
In answer to the question from my colleague, there would be two options that would be available to the Government of Canada. One, if Ukraine was recognized-I prefer not to use the word "state", I prefer the word "country"-as a separate country, then of course it would ask for diplomatic recognition here and diplomatic relations would be set up by the government. This act here would not affect that at all.
What this act would affect would be that if Ukraine became, if I could use the word under the legislation, a sub-unit of the Soviet Union, and then Ukraine would allow provincial representatives from Ontario, for example, or Alberta to Ukraine, then that act would allow us to recognize Ukraine under this act and then we would establish diplomatic relations with it.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext: Yes, but looking at the interpretation section, Madam Chairman, of political subdivision, would the minister tell the House if by political subdivision, as written, it means that Ukraine or the Russian Federation or the Baltics are for purposes of this act considered now, if passed today, to be political subdivisions of the U.S.S.R.?

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext: Madam Chairman, the Baltic States are not a subdivision. They are not recognized as a subdivision. With regard to Ukraine, the decision then would be, depending on the referendum and a decision of the people, a decision by the government with regard to diplomatic recognition then, depending on the referendum. The answer is not with regard to the Baltic States. They have been recognized by the government already.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I have three questions to ask. I think I will put them on this clause because they will fit.
One question is the matter of attaching the various conventions that you have put in this part of the bill. I would like to hear the minister's comments on whether at some point in time there are going to be disputes between those things which are printed as part of the bill, that is to say drafted as the normal law that we
Government Orders
would see, and those things that are interpreted out of the various conventions that are attached to the bill. Could we have some kind of clarification as to which will win the day? Does the convention, which is kind of an international agreement on how to do things, supersede any opinion that you might have in terms of drafting the rest of the legislation which you have printed here?

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, the legislation is both in C-27 and the potential of conflict with the Vienna conventions.
I am advised that many sections of the Vienna conventions are force of law in Canada. We do not anticipate problems between this bill and what is in the Vienna conventions, and those sections which are part of Canadian law. Obviously, if there was one, then the courts would decide.
By virtue of section 12, by virtue of the regulation section, that allows the government to have the regulations. As my hon. friend would hope and as I would hope, surely the government would draft the regulations under the law, that the regulations which would be drafted under this section certainly would have to fall under the general laws that are either in this or in the two Vienna conventions that apply. I hope they are.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, that might clarify some of the definition problems that we have been discussing about what is a state and what is not.
The second area that I wanted to explore just a touch is there is a great deal of the use of the word reciprocity here. My understanding is that that is just a general principle that is used. It also would lead one to believe that at some point in time, if one could get an agreement with another jurisdiction that went well beyond what might be contained in either of these conventions or this law, that nation or that jurisdiction might in fact have privileges that would extend well past what is enclosed or contemplated in any of these conventions or this act.
Could we hear the minister's comments on that?

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for his question.
When we talk about reciprocity, of course we are bound by the legislation that we have. We do agree with two sections, one in the Vienna Diplomatic Convention,

October 4, 1991
Government Orders
section 47, which talks about reciprocity and non-discrimination, and section 72, page 52 of our bill, which talks about consuls.
People who are considered diplomats get just about every immunity or privilege they could possibly get. There may be difficulties-I do not know if you could call them difficulties-but certainly the issue can be raised and has been raised by some that in certain cases consulates should have a type of immunity which would be similar to that of a diplomat. I am told that that is the case between the United States, the U.K., the Soviet Union, and China.
I am advised we have had one request from one government to modify the normal consulate privilege and immunities that they get and External Affairs is looking at it. It is done, I gather, in the normal course of business by External Affairs.
On the whole we are satisfied that the system we have in place is good, but does not prevent other immunities from being granted if done always in a reciprocal way.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I appreciate that this is pretty complicated stuff for us to be trying to deal with here on the floor without a lot of staff around, but I would like to hear comments on the power of the various ministers. I will put it in this context. The Secretary of State is mentioned and earlier the Minister of Finance is mentioned. There is clearly some ministerial powers that will be interpreted subsequently by one or more ministers of the Crown.
Is it the government's contention that where a conflict should arise, one or more of the ministers may extend the powers or may go the other way and curtail such powers. I would like to hear a little bit of an explanation as to how the government envisages that would work. I would be reluctant to be quite so enthusiastic about the bill if I thought that one person subsequently could rewrite this. I am not concerned at all that someone has to interpret particular circumstances, but I am concerned at how broad the powers given to the ministers are under this bill.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Two ministers are concerned with this legislation; first, the Secretary of State for External Affairs who, under this legislation, keeps the same powers that a minister has under other legislation. The legislation does not increase the powers of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The powers of the secretary of state are not increased with the proviso which I told
my hon. friend a few minutes ago when I was talking about consulates. That is the same.
What is new in the legislation, with regard to my hon. friend's question about powers, to use that word, of ministers, is that the Minister of Finance would have the authority to make decisions with regard to certain tax rolls in the diplomatic community. For example, if it will be to the mutual advantage of both countries to have certain diplomats exempt from certain taxes that would be done by the Minister of Finance. I believe that would be a reasonable thing for the Minister of Finance to do.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, the other issue I raised in the debate was of course that the bill is silent on the question of how an office of a political subdivision would become recognized as such. Again, in the Vienna Convention, Article 4 reads;
1.	The sending State must make certain that the agrement of the receiving State has been given for the person it proposes to accredit as head of the mission to that State.
2.	The receiving State is not obliged to give reasons to the sending State for a refusal of agrement.
Let us take the example of a diplomat from Ukraine who will come, let us say, to a consular office in Toronto, Ontario. The Secretary State for External Affairs has accepted this person's accreditation, but the subdivision state, in this case Ontario, does not accept this person to work in the Toronto consular office because it felt that this person had Communist ties in the past or whatever.
So at the federal level we are saying: "Yes, this person is acceptable to serve in the consular office in Toronto", but the Ontario government is saying; "No, sorry, we cannot accept this person". I do not think the bill addresses this issue, the process of actually setting up a consular office in a subdivision of Canada.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, my hon. friend from Parkdale-High Park is correct. The bill is silent on the issue because it was not the intention of the federal government to give a role in the recognition of a person from the Ukraine to the provincial government. If New York State wants to have someone in the City of Toronto, the federal government would recognize whoever went there. But we would not recognize someone from New York to Toronto unless we had been told by Queen's Park ahead of time that it would receive reciprocity in New York City. The decision of recognition is a federal one but we are not going to do it unless Queen's Park asks us and says that it wants reciprocity or have obtained reciprocity.

We do not believe there will be a problem with that.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
In crossing the country and asking for input into our Constitution, one of the big concerns expressed is the division of powers-which powers will go to the federal government, which powers will go to the provincial governments and which powers will be shared. Does the minister not think that since we are passing a new bill this should be spelled out? If it is a shared decision the bill should say so. If it is federal jurisdiction the bill should say so.
When we pass legislation today we are passing legislation for the next 20, 50 years. Let us get it right the first time.

subtopic: FOREIGN MISSIONS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I see my friend's point but we feel that the bill is clear on that issue with the interpretation of section 6.(1). The bill says that the Secretary of State for External Affairs may, for the purpose of according to that office, make sure that reciprocity is offered in the other jurisdictions. As a result of the wording of section 6 that can be the only interpretation.
The government always likes to take a co-operative approach to these issues. I am sure discussions would be held with the respective provinces if there was a request for that.
